opus-5.5.text:
Thank you for having me. I think the way intelligence interacts with the environment can be understood along a spectrum.

At one end you have what I'd call disembodied intelligence, which is essentially what large language models are today. They interact with the world through text, through symbols. Their "environment" is the internet, human-written knowledge, and the conversations they have with us. That form of intelligence is extraordinarily powerful at abstraction, reasoning, and recombining knowledge, but it never touches the physical world directly. It never has to deal with friction, gravity, or the fact that an object might slip out of your hand.

At the other end you have embodied intelligence, which is what I work on. Here the agent has a body, it has sensors, it has actuators, and it has to close the loop with the physical world in real time. Every action changes the state of the environment, and the environment pushes back. This creates a very different kind of intelligence. Much of it isn't verbal at all. Think about how a child learns to grasp a cup or walk. That knowledge is not stored as sentences; it's stored as sensorimotor patterns, as an intuitive physics.

In between there are interesting intermediate forms, for example agents acting in simulated or digital environments, like controlling a computer, playing games, or navigating a virtual world. They take actions and get feedback, but the feedback is cleaner and cheaper than in the real world.

What I find most important is that the form of interaction shapes the form of intelligence. Language models learned from a massive corpus that humans had already produced, so data was abundant. Embodied agents don't have that luxury. There is no "internet of robot actions." So we have to think hard about where the data comes from: simulation, synthetic data, human demonstrations, and eventually the robot's own interaction with the world.

My belief is that true general intelligence will need both. The language side gives you high-level understanding, planning, and common sense about goals. The embodied side gives you grounding, the ability to actually do things and to understand what words like "heavy," "fragile," or "push gently" really mean. The interesting frontier right now is how to connect these two, so that a robot can take abstract understanding from a large model and turn it into precise, robust physical action, and in turn, how physical experience can make the model's understanding of the world more real.

r002.rationale: It contrasts disembodied, simulated, and embodied interaction, but does not distinguish them by temporal horizon.

r003.rationale: It describes bodies, sensors, and actuators, but does not distinguish bodily interaction by available movement dimensionality.

fable-5.1.text:
Thank you, Xiaojun. I think of it as a spectrum of embodiment, really.

At one end you have intelligence that lives purely in symbols. A language model is the obvious example. It takes in text, it produces text, and the environment it interacts with is a stream of tokens. It never touches anything. But it still has an environment, and it still acts on it. When you ask it a question and it answers, that answer changes what you do next, so there is a feedback loop, just a very slow and indirect one.

Then you move toward intelligence that perceives but doesn't act physically. A vision system, a recommendation engine. It sees the world, in some sense, but its outputs are decisions or labels rather than movements. The interaction is still mostly one-directional.

And at the other end you have embodied intelligence, which is where my own work sits. A robot has to perceive, decide, and then actually move something, and the world pushes back. If you grasp a cup wrong, it falls. If you push a door, the door resists. The environment is not a passive dataset anymore. It is an adversary, or at least an indifferent partner. And that changes everything about how the intelligence has to be built, because errors compound in real time and you cannot just sample again.

What I find interesting is that these are not really separate kinds of intelligence. They are the same underlying thing, prediction and control, operating at different levels of contact with reality. Humans do all of them at once. We talk, we see, we move. The question for the field right now is whether we can get a single system to do that too, or whether the physical layer demands something fundamentally different. My intuition is that the physical layer teaches you things the symbolic layer never will. You learn what weight is, what friction is, what it means for something to be out of reach. Those concepts are everywhere in language, but language only borrowed them from bodies.

astra-6.text:
I think intelligence takes different forms partly because different agents have different ways of interacting with their environment. A person, a robot, and a software system receive different information and have different actions available to them. So what counts as intelligent behavior depends on that relationship.

One useful way to look at it is as a loop: you perceive something, take an action, observe what changes, and adjust. Sometimes that loop is very immediate, like keeping your balance. Sometimes it involves planning—imagining what might happen before you act. And sometimes it involves other people, where you need to communicate and understand their intentions.

These forms aren’t necessarily separate. Picking up a cup, for example, involves seeing its position, anticipating its weight, controlling your hand, and correcting your grip as you feel it. Something that looks simple can require several kinds of intelligence working together.

So I would understand intelligence less as a single ability and more as the capacity to adapt your interaction with the world: to learn what matters, predict the consequences of your actions, and change your behavior when your expectations turn out to be wrong.

sol-6.1.text:
I think intelligence takes different forms partly because the environments and tasks are different. If you’re answering a question, you can work primarily with language and abstract knowledge. But if you’re picking up a cup, you have to connect perception with action: where is the cup, how should you approach it, how much force should you apply, and what do you do if it starts to slip?

In that setting, intelligence is a continuous loop. You observe, act, see how the environment changes, and adjust. Your body matters, too. A hand’s shape and the way it makes contact can make a task easier, so intelligence isn’t only about computation in isolation; it also emerges through the relationship between the agent and its environment.

What connects these forms, I think, is the ability to use experience to act effectively under uncertainty. The interesting question is how abstract reasoning and this very concrete, physical feedback can support each other.
